title: Merge Two Sorted Lists
statement:
Two log shippers each send you a singly linked list of event timestamps, already sorted from oldest to newest. You must splice them into one sorted list without copying the nodes, so the downstream reader sees one ordered stream.

A linked list is given as a Python list of its node values, from head to tail; [] is the empty list. Return a list in the same format. In an interview you would get the head node and return a head node; to practise that, build the nodes, move the next pointers, then read the values back.

Write def solution(a, b) where a and b are both sorted in non-decreasing order. Return the values of one linked list that contains every node of both, in non-decreasing order. Equal values from both lists all appear. Lists can have 100,000 nodes each, so avoid recursion.

examples.why: Take the smaller front each time; equal values from both lists all stay.
One list is empty, so the answer is the other list.

constraints: each list is sorted in non-decreasing order

think.q: Which node comes first in the merged list?
think.a: The smaller of the two heads. Both lists are sorted, so the smallest remaining value is always at the front of one of them. After you take it, the same question repeats on what is left.

Fronts 1 and 1: take either 1. Fronts 2 and 1: take 1. Fronts 2 and 3: take 2. Fronts 4 and 3: take 3. Fronts 4 and 4: take 4. One list is empty: attach the other, the last 4. Result 1, 1, 2, 3, 4, 4.

think.q: What is the first idea that works?
think.a: Put every value in one array and sort it, then build a new list. That is O((n + m) log(n + m)), it ignores that the inputs are already sorted, and it makes new nodes instead of splicing the existing ones.

A dummy head plus a tail pointer. The dummy is a placeholder node in front of the result, so the first real node needs no special case. Compare the two fronts, hook the smaller one onto tail, advance that list and the tail. When one list runs out, hook on the rest of the other in one step.

1. Build both lists. dummy = ListNode(0), tail = dummy.
  2. While both lists have nodes: pick the front with the smaller value (the first list on a tie), set tail.next to it, advance that list, set tail = tail.next.
  3. Set tail.next to whichever list is not empty.
  4. Return the values from dummy.next.

Both lists empty. One list empty. Every value of one list smaller than every value of the other (the loop ends at once and the rest is attached). Equal values across the lists. Negative values. Lists of very different lengths.

hints: The smallest remaining value is always at the front of one of the two lists. Take it, and repeat.
Start the result with a dummy node and keep a tail pointer to its last node. Then adding a node is always tail.next = node, even for the first one.
When one list is used up, you do not need to loop over the other: tail.next = a if a is not None else b attaches all of it.
explain:
Example 1, a = 1 → 2 → 4 and b = 1 → 3 → 4:

  • 1 vs 1: tie, take a's 1. Result 1.
  • 2 vs 1: take b's 1. Result 1, 1.
  • 2 vs 3: take 2. Then 4 vs 3: take 3. Then 4 vs 4: take a's 4.
  • a is empty, so attach the rest of b, the last 4. Result [1, 1, 2, 3, 4, 4].

Each comparison moves one node into place, so the loop runs at most n + m times. The dummy node removes the special case of an empty result: without it you would need an if head is None branch for the first node. No node is copied; only next pointers change.
complexity: O(n + m) time, O(1) extra space beyond the nodes

tests.label: second list empty
tests.why: the first list is returned as is

tests.label: no overlap
tests.why: the loop ends early and the rest is attached
